name: Ritlecitinib (Litfulo)

lead: Ritlecitinib (Litfulo) is a daily pill from Pfizer approved in 2023 for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks hair follicles, in people 12 and older. It is used to regrow hair lost in patches.

It irreversibly blocks JAK3 and TEC-family kinases, dampening immune signalling involved in the attack on follicles, although the label says the importance of each target to its effect is not known. It is not approved for ordinary male or female pattern hair loss, and no published trial has tested it there.

paras: It is a prescription-only oral drug taken daily under medical supervision for alopecia areata. It was approved by the FDA in June 2023, then in the EU in September 2023 and Canada in November 2023.

The label carries a boxed warning for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major cardiovascular events and thrombosis. Common effects include headache, diarrhea and acne. It reportedly costs about US$49,000 a year.

angle.text: Ritlecitinib is a prescription drug for severe alopecia areata, where it is used to regrow hair lost in patches by calming the immune attack on follicles. Hair-loss communities discuss it mainly as a separate condition from pattern baldness. It is not studied or approved for pattern hair loss.

lead: Ritlecitinib, sold as Litfulo and developed by Pfizer, is an oral kinase inhibitor prescribed for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, in adults and adolescents aged 12 and older.[1][2] The US label describes it as irreversibly inhibiting Janus kinase 3 (JAK3) and the TEC family of kinases, and notes that the relevance of inhibiting specific enzymes to its therapeutic effect is not currently known.[1]

It was first approved by the US FDA in June 2023, followed by the European Union in September 2023 and Canada in November 2023.[2][2] It is a prescription-only drug and is not indicated for androgenetic (pattern) hair loss, the form of hair loss most discussed in looksmaxxing communities.[1] Its label carries a boxed warning covering serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.[1]
infobox: Severe alopecia areata, age 12 and over

paras: The US label lists severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents 12 years and older as the indication. It states that use together with other JAK inhibitors, biologic immunomodulators, cyclosporine or other potent immunosuppressants is not recommended.[1]

Beyond alopecia areata, registered studies have explored ritlecitinib in non-segmental vitiligo (a phase 3 programme), keloids, chronic spontaneous urticaria and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; these are investigational uses.[3][4][5][6]

Per the label, ritlecitinib binds irreversibly at the ATP-binding site of JAK3 and of the TEC kinase family, blocking cytokine-induced STAT phosphorylation mediated by JAK3-dependent receptors and signalling by TEC-dependent immune receptors.[1] Grokipedia describes the drug as sparing other Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, TYK2) in biochemical assays and reducing cytotoxic activity of natural killer cells and CD8 T cells, which it connects with hair regrowth; that source is AI-generated and should be read with caution.[7]
Grokipedia reports rapid oral absorption with peak levels in about an hour and a terminal half-life of roughly 1.3 to 2.3 hours.[7]

The most common adverse reactions listed on the label (incidence 1% or more) include headache, diarrhea, acne, rash, urticaria, folliculitis, fever, atopic dermatitis and dizziness.[1] The boxed warning describes increased risk of serious bacterial, fungal, viral and opportunistic infections including tuberculosis, along with mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.[1]

Warnings and precautions also cover hypersensitivity, hypoglycemia in people with diabetes, laboratory abnormalities (lymphocyte and platelet counts to be checked before starting) and avoidance of live vaccines.[1] The label states that animal studies caused fetotoxicity and malformations at high exposures and that human pregnancy data are insufficient; a pregnancy exposure registry exists.[1]

Approval rested on the ALLEGRO programme, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b/3 trial (NCT03732807) in about 718 participants aged 12 and over with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss, run at 128 sites in 18 countries.[2] Grokipedia states that the trial showed significantly greater scalp hair coverage than placebo at 24 weeks.[7]

Later registrations include real-world retrospective studies in US patients with severe alopecia areata and phase 3 work in vitiligo.[8][9][4] Several phase 1 pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers have also been registered.[10] No published trial has examined ritlecitinib for androgenetic alopecia.

Pfizer developed the drug, which is also known by the code PF-06651600; it was the second JAK inhibitor approved for alopecia areata, after baricitinib.[2][7] Wikipedia reports an annual US list price of about US$49,000.[2]
